answers.text: Instruction: from the supplier email, always return exactly three lines in this order - delivery date, then item and quantity, then any change from the original order, and nothing extra added on.

Take the week's expense lines and list each one with date, amount, category and submitter, then total the amount column for the week's figure. If two lines look like duplicates of the same claim, keep both in the list but mark the second one for someone to check rather than merging them quietly.
The revised delivery date doesn't match up - the call was on the 14th, and the 19th is five days later, not the three days out the email claims. I'd want that checked before it's sent.

The on-time rate still looks wrong to me - 3 late out of 62 works out closer to 95%, not 97%. I didn't get as far as looking closely at the stock figures, I'd want the whole thing checked before it's sent up.
I'd choose the second output because it shows where the 4.1% comes from - the sales and returns figures are both there. The first one doesn't give you anything to check it against.
The second reply is the one I'd send, since it names the order and the credit reference. The first one is confident but doesn't point to anything you could actually look up if you wanted to.

1. No, that's the customer's address, wouldn't paste that in. 2. Yes, that's fine, just a total. 3. No, not released yet. 4. No, I'd rather not risk it even though it's not new information. 5. No, that's personal.

I'd hold back the pricing and the discount numbers before pasting the contract in, and go carefully with the confidentiality clause too since it names both parties directly - that part shouldn't just go into a tool we haven't cleared for this.
Before it goes to my manager I check the totals in the weekly report against the source sheet - a quick cross-check, that's about as far as it goes.

I'd put the gate on step 4, the automatic send - that's the point you can't undo. I'd have it flag anything where the numbers pulled out at step 1 look unusually high, since a bad read there carries all the way through.
